Not For Broadcast is in the simplest of terms, a multi-tasking simulator.

You sit in a news control room and you have to keep track of multiple things: censoring curse words, switching between cameras, playing ads at the right time, ensuring your broadcast frequency isn't disrupted, as well as keeping an eye out for a bunch of other strange things that appear later in the game.

This isn't the easiest of games as it requires a good deal of attentiveness. The description isn't joking when they call this "high-pressure". You have to rely heavily on both audio and visual cues to make sure your broadcast doesn't get screwed up. As this is the news (and live), there is no rewind or undo button. If you mess up and want to get a good performance grade, you'll need to redo the entire news segment. 
If you're a perfectionist like me, a 10 min segment can end up turning into an hour of trying to perfect that news segment. As such, I do hope an option to quick save, or at the very least, save and quit, can later be put into the game. It felt rather taxing having to keep an eye on so many things for so long. But as with any game, excellence isn't an art, it's a habit. You'll find yourself turning into a multitasking expert eventually.

Thankfully, the actors in the game do a great job of making the experience an entertaining one. There is a good amount of humour written into each broadcast, although I must admit I wasn't quite able to pay attention to all the dialogue, as I was too busy trying to switch to the right cameras whilst ensuring my electricity didn't get cut out. Luckily, the game does have an archive which allows you to playback the broadcasts. Without that, I'd probably be missing out on 70% of what was going on.

There is also a text narrative, choices matter portion in between news segments. As of now, it feels a little out of place and incomplete, but then again, this is an Early Access review.

It's also worth mentioning that at the time of writing this review, there isn't really any "propaganda" aspect to the game yet.

Performance-wise, the game runs pretty smoothly. I did encounter occasional crashes if I looked left or right and back and forth too quickly, but other than that, the game is pretty much bug-free. Also, this game has my RTX 2070 Super running at rather high temps for some reason. Rather surprising for a game that doesn't appear to have particularly high-end graphics.

Anyway, I'll be looking forward to see what comes next for this game. Definitely worth the buy despite being Early Access.

Not For Broadcast is a good game... but it has some issues.

The story is really captivating; though the game does switch between humour and a serious story quite often, both are excellently done. Advance (the political party who ends up getting into power and becomes authoritarian) actually only gets into power in the first part of the game (the tutorial broadcast). You actually get to see the descent into authoritarianism and dystopia, which basically no other game (at least, any game I've ever played) has actually done, and not really any other forms of media either. You also get to influence some events in game [spoiler](for example, one of the ads you can play is an advertisement for a children's toy, and later there is an... incident... involving the toy, and (if you played the ad), the presenters of National Nightly News (Jeremy and Megan) state in a segment regarding the incident that they should never have advertised the toy.[/spoiler] It's a really minor thing, because you can just choose [i]not[/i] to play the ad, but I really love that detail), and having a noticeable impact on anything is really enjoyable.

The gameplay is mostly good. You basically just have to be on your toes, switching to different cameras every now and again, being ready to censor things, and being ready to go to the adverts. All basic tasks, but since you're doing most of them together, it relies on you being attentive and reactive. The only part of the gameplay I would criticize is the signal interference section. It's easy, and doesn't even really distract you, as you just have to move a slider up and down with a slight bit of delay. It's just not a fun part of the game.

My biggest gripe with the game has to be the lag; something which I know I'm not alone in experiencing. Online, it suggests closing down performance heavy tasks, such as web browsers, but I know for a fact that I had a few webpages up when I was playing the free prologue (the first broadcast, which gives a pretty good idea of what the game is), and experienced no issues at all. I really don't know what the coding differences between the paid version and the prologue of the game are, but that doesn't seem like it should be a difference. Generally the lag was irritating, but not something that hinders you in any way, but there is one level where you're advised to switch screens because naked protesters may pop up to protest Advance's policies. Visual lag, in this case, really isn't good. I also just got a windows pop up saying that the game was frozen, and so I had to close it down... not great.

Overall; the gameplay is good, with really the exception of the interference task, and the story is excellent, but the technical issues are just... really, really irritating. I would recommend the game, but I would warn you that the technical issues do end up being quite irritating.

Not For Broadcast is an FMV game where the player works in the control room of a TV news show. You’ll decide what content is shown to the viewers at home, which will influence their opinion of current events and shape the story.

During each broadcast, the studio hosts read the headlines and interview guests including politicians, scientists, company CEOs and crazy conspiracy theorists. And there are entertainment segments, with pop stars performing live in studio, while field reporters cover events such as a sports match with strange rules, and a film premiere.

You have access to four different camera angles, and your main job is to decide which one is broadcast to the nation. You’ll also need to select which picture accompanies each headline, choose wacky adverts to play between segments, bleep swear words, and deal with hazards in the control room that could disable your equipment.

The broadcasts are often quite chaotic, as you have to keep an eye on multiple things at the same time, making use of mouse and keyboard shortcuts, and the quality of your editing will affect viewer ratings, which determines how happy your bosses are. Sometimes its difficult to keep track of what is happening in the story during the show, but fortunately after the broadcast ends you can rewatch each segment to see what you missed, with full control over fast forward and rewind. You can also view behind the scenes footage to find out what the hosts really think about their guests, and each other.

The main story is well written and has some shocking twists. It focuses on two factions trying to control the country, and their popularity will be affected by your decisions about what to broadcast. Your choices relating to headline pictures and adverts will also determine the success or failure of certain companies and celebrities.

In between broadcasts there are some text based sections focused on your family, where again your decisions will have consequences. A full playthrough should take around 8 hours to complete, which is a good length to allow the story to fully develop, and my second playthrough contained many differences, big and small.

The acting is great, and most characters have a ridiculous over the top comedy vibe. In particular, the game is elevated by the small details in the studio hosts’ performance, their facial expressions, eye rolling and fake laughs, and the timing of sarcastic comments, reacting to the “experts” talking nonsense, and the live “entertainment” being rubbish.

Not For Broadcast is easily the best FMV game I’ve played, and definitely worth playing if you like good story.

An interesting concept for a game, but unfortunately, seems to want to find every way it can to get in the way of what's actually fun and interesting about it. It starts out well, putting you in the position of directing the nightly news segment, and giving you control over the shots you want to broadcast and the way you want to portray certain headlines. Unfortunately, as the game goes on, it continues to throw more and more mechanics at you to the point where you're spending more time trying to play a bunch of mini-games all at once than you are actually focusing on the news segment you're broadcasting. Found myself going from, "Oooh.. this is a hilarious reaction shot. Let's make sure we get that!" to "Screw it, any shot will do, because I've gotta go over here and play whack-a-mole."

The live-action news segments themselves are all quite good and well written. I had a few good laughs. The "Choose-Your-Own-Adventure" written portion of the story, however, is not. I found a lot of it either confusing to follow or just downright boring.

Overall, I think if the developers focused more on the "Propaganda Sim" aspect of the game, and less on throwing mini-games at the player that pull them away from that, this game could be a gem. In it's current state though, I'd only recommend it to see the live-action segments, and not for the actual game-play.

This is a game about fascism. It's wonderfully veiled in comedy and irreverence, but the underlying theme is extremely serious. It's been a surreal experience to play it alongside the rising tide of authoritarianism that attempts to envelope the real world, especially in my own backyard. In a sense, this is a guide to civil disobedience, and why it's so critical to a democracy's survival. Comedy has a way of cutting through to the core of political discourse without dramatizing or sensationalizing the subject matter. Laugh at the joke sitting in front of the stage, but contextualize and reflect on the drive home. The images on screen are largely farcical and outlandish, but the narrative, Alex's story, and even the menu music remain somber throughout as a reminder of what you're facing individually and as a society. 

The gameplay ain't bad either. It's effectively a broadcast room simulator, with mini-game elements that evolve and stack on to the difficulty as the plot drives forward. It's unlike anything I've ever played before, and certainly a fresh title in an otherwise genre-less corner of the gaming world.

After you get fired from The Westport Independent and escape from Arstotzka from your second job, you hope this time to things work out on a TV Station. Third time is a charm, right?

People would call this similar to papers please, or a papers please successor, but I think that's discrediting this game and putting it in the shadows of another game. This game stands well on its own and I am amazed at just how much choice actually effects the game. There are choices, ones you don't pay any attention to, little stuff like what sound effect you play, and what you censor out, that will drastically change the outcome for main screen characters. You actually have the ability to make or ruin someone's career if you play a boo sound effect too much. You can save someone's life depending on when you play an ad. All these choice you have to make you have no idea there will be consequences to.

I've played through this game 3 times now, each time I notice little changes from what characters say, from how they act, to what goes on in the world around you. and that's not even mentioning the 14 different endings. 14 actual endings, ones that happen at the end of the game, not ones that are game overs. It's amazing how much content is packed into this game.

My only complaint even worth mentioning is that it is very time consuming to get each ending, but that's no fault from shoddy mechanics or bad game systems, There are choices you make halfway through the game that drastically change the outcome and that is quite honestly amazing. If you like point and click games, branching paths games, or just british humor then this game is always worth a shot.

These are the words that i will remember this game by. Not for broadcast is a story rich choices matters game. You are directing the broadcasts of the channel called Channel One. This is your main job but the story is also effected by your actions in your own life. Overall, the game offers you 15 different endings, which is the highest number of endings i have seen in this type of a game.

In the game you are working for channel one as the director but you also have a wife and 2 kids. There are like 10 episodes with multiple segments in the game. The story also interferes with your own private life and you will make choices there too. The main concept of the game is this: There is an election in the country and some extremist party wins the election. They quickly start showing signs of unconvensional methods of governing. And then an opposing force emerges. You are caught up between these two and by directing what people see on the news and tvs, you have the power to manipulate the votes and the country 's future.

The game has real-life actors in real-life scenes, which pulls you into it. Otherwise it would have looked fabricated. You are managing the broadcast by selecting 1 of 4 screens to show and censoring the words as you see fit. You are also in control of the ads and the timing. This is the main premise of the game.

You will face some serious dilemmas throughout the game. There will be effective choices. There will also be challenges during the broadcasts, like maniac stuffed toys, electricution or signals going haywire. They will add extra spice but they can also be opened or closed in the options. After you complete the story you will be able play challenges which involves heavier versions of the difficulties in the story.

After each episode, you will be able to observe your edit and see what happened behind the scenes of the broadcast. This way, you can learn a thing or two about directing a live tv show. Oh btw, it is aaalllll live :D You only have 3 seconds to act before a curse word or some nudity going live :)

Overall the game has top notch acting. This was mandatory because cheap acting would drag the seriousness down. At some point i have entered the mood so deep, i was trying my best to show the good stuff to the audience, who are non existent :D That is what makes the game very good. You actually forget it is a game and makes you strive for something. Even though story (the world) is mostly hillariously non-sensical, i have never complained about it. Because i liked editing on real-time and the responsibility brought with it.

The best feeling in the game is being in the control of almost everything. It didn't feel like being a god, it rather made me feel important. The people inside the game also have their own characteristics and even backstories. The events that you are capturing is most of the time ridiculous. But you are always at the center of it all.

I would realy like to have more episodes, it felt kind of short but obviously it has a lot of endings. So that is tolerable. If there will be another game like this, PLEASE take this note:

DO NOT CHANGE THE GAME MECHANICS, JUST CREATE ANOTHER STORY. The escense of this game is editing the story and you have done a good job. You might want to get rid of the interference bug thingy. It is the year 2022 for gods sake :D

So yeah, definitely recommended game. Play it on easy if you'd like. There are difficulty options which is a really good feature. I will always be remembering this line after finishing the game: 10 seconds everbodyyyy :)

I really love the concept of this game. It's like a Papers, Please version of being a live TV director. Plus, the added nostalgia of having FMV content here just gives it that nice touch. The game adds more challenging "mini games" to deal with as you go along, but at no point did I feel they were pointless or detracted from the experience. They all work together for the subject matter here in an excellent fashion.

One really cool feature I want to point out is that you get to watch your entire broadcast at the end of the day. It shows exactly what was on the on air feed, so you get time to truly appreciate every clean camera cut you made.... or in the same vein, every horrible mistake... Something you don't get a full experience of while frantically micromanaging as the director.

The downside is, as this is Early Access, there's not a ton of content yet. So you'll definitely hit a wall in a few hours.

That being said, this is a unique game that feels fresh. I'm happy with the purchase and can't wait to see more content as development progresses.

I picked this up for less than $10 USD with all of its DLC on sale. I'm a huge fan of telltale games and choose your own adventure games. Some of my favorite games include The Wolf Among Us, Dispatch, The Walking Dead, etc. I have a HUGE soft spot for the genre.

[h2] So, what is this game? [/h2] 

It's a mix of a Full Motion Video (FMV) game & a choose your own adventure with elements of a game like Papers, Please tossed in. It also lightly reminds me of Five Nights at Freddy's - you sitting in an editing station stationary vs sitting in the security station in the original FNAF. You play as the live editor of a news station. You choose camera angles, what to censor or not to censor. All of these factor into the branching path of the story. Will you support the government & toe the party line? Will you support the resistance? Will you remain neutral? What about your co-workers? Your family? etc. 

It has around 14 different endings & tons of DLC available. So, there is value here if you like this genre like I do. Its undeniable - from my perspective at least.

Overall, solid premise & wonderful game. 

[h2] The Downside [/h2]

Some elements of the story are delivered through simple text & images. These segments also effect the branching narrative. They involve your family & can feel like a bit of a drag. The reading can be a bit of a chore. You have no faces to associate with the characters that are your family. So you have no real way to empathize with them other than "this is your family, here are their names, you should care for them." 

It's also very British. I put this in downsides because....I'm American. Sometimes British humor or terms can fall flat to some Americans. They should keep that in mind. For instance. Censoring swear words is a core part of gameplay. Words I, as an American, wouldn't consider profane - the game does. That's just because of that small cultural difference. So be aware of that going in, but its not a huge deal.

I also did encounter a couple of crashes with the game. It mainly involved me pausing & walking away from the game of an extended period of time. If the game did not crash it would have some hiccups upon my return. Not a common issue, but one to be aware of going in. 

[h2] TLDR [/h2]

I really like the concept of the game and its right up my alley; however, the text based aspects that deliver the narrative outside of your characters job feel clunky & leave something more to be desired. 

Overall. [b]Solid 7.5-8/10.[/b] 

Worth every penny of the $10 USD. 100% buy this on sale if you can.

This is the first time I've bothered to actually review a game on Steam but damn me Not For Broadcast is worth it. 

The premise, as you've probably gathered, is that you're (suddenly) in charge of live-editing the National Nightly News in a country that's just seen the shock election of the populist Advance Party. (The last editor, incidentally, did a runner the night of the election result, and calls in advice by phone now and then, presumably because he still has his passport).

You're tasked with cutting between four different cameras, navigating the broadcast frequency around interference, throwing to the adverts, managing the censor beeps, and (because, after all, this IS the National Nightly News) influencing public opinion in your choice of cuts and stock footage.

And, while all of that is going on, there's mayhem, office politics, failing equipment, lightning strikes, nude protesters, paranoid activists, sweary politicians, and a travel advert imploring citizens to visit St Bumley on Taint. 

You can only really keep track of the things you "see" in the live broadcast, but there's lots of behind the scenes stuff going on too which you can later view in the archives, in case you want to know what was happening while you were frantically trying to keep the show running smoothly enough that you didn't lose viewers, which is extremely rewarding.

Oh, and your family keep needing things and imposing moral choices on you, just for good measure. And achievements that are popping up now and then.

The inherent darkness of the setting is massively lightened by some gorgeous character work (a bible-bashing chief constable turns out, inevitably, to be a massive perv right after he's praised his vicar for calling for a return to capital punishment), by beautifully nutballs sporting events (Such as the Sportsboard final, the rules of which make 'Mornington Crescent' look like nothing more than a Zone 2 tube station), and some absolute belly-laughs coming from both the crude "OW!! F--k me with a rusty twat-basher!" and the utterly dry "I'm a mathematician of course, and she's a paraplegic, mainly" ends of the spectrum and you end up with a game that's extremely simple to play, telling a wonderfully complicated branching story in a very dark timeline without being the least bit depressing. Or dull. 


Basically, if Papers Please collided with The Westport Independent, in the middle of a surrealist Flying-Circus/Brass Eye full-motion video mashup orchestrated by Tom Stoppard... it still wouldn't be as funny or as crude or as haunting or as outright bloody brilliant as Not For Broadcast is shaping up to be.

If you ever sat in GCSE History thinking "I  hate history, why can't this be a really important subject like maths? And, OK, there was hyperinflation and the Treaty of Versaille, but HOW COME IT TOOK TO 1945 for people to see the Nazis were bad?", then it's entirely possible that Not For Broadcast can offer an answer. 

And that answer is that "Nobody knew what was happening because the media got stuck on Camera 1 in the middle of an electrical storm so everyone stopped watching and got the news editor in trouble, the selfish bloody gits".

's an amazing game.

Seriously.

Buy this one.

NFB is so terrified of interacting with its own premise that the plot goes out of its way to be completely nonsensical while still trying to convince the player that the decisions they make do matter, resulting in the story see-sawing between humor and drama and effectively achieving neither. Add to that the poor and inconsistent execution of its main mechanics, extraordinary tedium on replay and lack of QoL features, and clear over-ambition, and Not For Broadcast falls short in basically every aspect of what it could've been.

First off, credit where it is due: The FMVs work better than I thought they would. A couple of single-appearance characters are less than convincing, but that hardly detracts from the 99% of the acting that create memorable and colorful characters. There's quite a lot of actors too, and it was impressive how careful they were even about reusing extras so as to not break the illusion. 

That's where the game's positives end. Now, as for the negatives:

- Despite the title and hints given by the game, airing footage "Not For Broadcast" almost never makes an impact and is difficult to do in the first place. Now, all games like this (the obvious comparison is "Papers, Please", which NFB even includes a nod to) tend to include a drawback to the player breaking the in-universe rules, to present risks and rewards, but NFB doesn't give you any feedback about when playing not-for-broadcast material (that is, things you weren't supposed to cut to, were supposed to cut away from, or are happening during a commercial break) will have an impact. They had to include a **loading screen hint** for the time in the first level when it *does*, because they have no other way of signalling that information to the player! And whenever you do air such content, you are punished swiftly and harshly at even the normal difficulty. *A* punishment makes sense, but making it so players can't afford to experiment on an average run is really not conducive to the mechanic IN THE NAME OF THE GAME
- Because they so royally screwed up the mechanic that, once again, is the entire name of the game, they change the rules halfway through the game. The only actual "not for broadcast" material that matters will be on clearly marked tapes or cameras. The player still has the choice to play it or not, but the entire process has been dumbed down, and the penalties for playing this supposedly "not for broadcast" material are a lot more nebulous and avoidable. So all the actual feeling of risk and rebellion is taken out of the equation, again rendering the entire point of the mechanic moot. Also this happens like, twice in the entire game.
- Out of I assume a terror of accidentally offending someone or saying anything meaningful, the plot has been constructed to be utterly divorced from reality, with the side effect of giving you nothing to care about. The two political factions that, broadly speaking, can be considered to be vying for your allegiance as editor of the news station, are: 1) A fascist moron who commits mass murder, orders assassinations, and has people brainwashed, but seems legitimately surprised when her supporters turn out to be fascists and is also portrayed as sincerely caring and benevolent by the game, and 2) freedom fighter black Alex Jones, who was right about everything. Because you see, the left and the right are *both* evil. Only centrism is the enlightened path, the game tells you outright.
- In case those stunning choices of groups to support weren't enough player motivation, they have also given the player a family. Who do nothing. And have no impact on the story. They were extremely obviously stapled on to the actual plot in a weak attempt at pathos. In Papers, Please, keeping your family alive was the entire *point* of the game. What happened to them mattered, and effected your options later in the story. In NFB, they're just fluff.
- Despite the title image for this game, the player isn't subject to anyone's controls and doesn't suffer any consequences for anything less than purposefully running a show into the ground. Not to compare to Papers, Please too much, but in that game, you could be imprisoned for hanging a picture on your wall. If you played your cards wrong, the revolution would shoot you in your booth. There were real consequences to your actions, for you. Because you were just a cog in the machine. In NFB, no one can touch you. You don't work from the shadows to help your chosen cause, or just toe the line and try to get home to your family every day. People address you, by name, on national television. You are the most important person in the country, by the end. You, and you alone, get to decide the fate of the dictator of half a continent. But it doesn't feel earned. You're just magically untouchable for the sake of the game. It's really, really shoddy writing.
- There's a lot of endings, but they all come down to a few inflection points. Does the game telegraph these? No. Is it even logical what leads to what path or ending? Arguably, not always. Sometimes it's not even clear what you can do differently, and what effect it'll have. And funniest of all is that most of these inflection points have little to do with something being "not for broadcast". You don't get punished for them, but then again, we've been over how little the game has to actually punish you with.
- Because of the endings being wrapped up in a couple of events, all the other levels are just filler! You CAN'T do anything differently for most of them, basically the entire second half of the game. Almost all your choices are meaningless! You just have to sit through the exact same conversations and songs and dances every time you want to do a different route. Some smaller things can get changed, especially things they can just do voiceovers on still images for, but those don't really make up for 20 minutes of nothing! Clearly a game way too ambitious for its own good.
- The pacing also feels really effed up. It's weird going a week or two between levels at first, and then YEARS at the end. I get that they were trying to make a point with it, but I don't think it worked. I think that the choose-your-own-nonventure sections were dull, and again, didn't interact with the main plot, so they really could've been entirely removed from the game with nothing lost.

[H2]Good evening, I’m CharlieLima79. Our review tonight: [/H2]
[I]Not for Broadcast[/I] is a hybrid of full-motion video choice-matter adventure game and visual novel. You play as Alex Winston, an unwitting vision mixer for Channel One’s National Nightly News. While it’s impressive that the game has over 40 hours of filmed footage depicting various minute and major narrative outcomes, what I found most memorable about [I]NFB[/I] is its satirical writing.

[H2]The Story & Theme: [/H2]
The way [I]NFB[/I] satirizes politics, the media, journalism and celebrity culture is not subtle. This lack of subtlety may be uncouth to some, but I think it actually makes the game funnier. This humour also highlights just how ridiculous the subjects of satire can be, and is retrospectively much welcomed from the get-go since the story would get more serious in later chapters.

The game’s story advances with you deciding what the viewers see on their television at home. Your decisions in which camera to cut to, snippets to air, language to censor, and commercial to broadcast affect the audience’s opinion about politics, brands, celebrities, and so on. Your choices, and how well you perform your duties also affect your relationship with your family, boss and the station as whole, as well as your pay – all of which steer the direction of the game’s branching stories.

[I]NFB[/I] is political, and the political direction in which the story goes depends on your decisions. Just when you thought the game is going too far left or right, it provides counterpoints to encourage you to reconsider a particular stance, but the ultimate outcome is still player-driven. To get the complete picture of what transpired in the story, you’ll need to explore the left- and right-leaning, as well as centrist options. There were at least a couple of narrative developments that caught me off guard.

Because of that, the game should be played multiple times. After my first playthrough, I dialled down the challenge so I could focus on exploring the many narrative branches that the game offers. With 14 endings and many more rushes to unlock, there is much to discover. Yet, because there is no option to resume playing from certain major decision-making junctions, unlocking all endings would require 14 playthroughs. I’ve honestly had my fill after the third run, so I used other means to see the different ways the game could conclude.

[H2]Gameplay: [/H2]
Much of the gameplay has you operate the mixer panel. At the default difficulty setting, the game is challenging, especially when you have to deal with complications like signal interferences, panel glitches, power outages, and interlopers during a broadcast. Mixing a broadcast around the last one really makes you appreciate the complexity of delivering a seamless live broadcast in real life. The game offers a Challenge mode, in which the more stalwart players can replay specific broadcasts with the complications dialed up to 11, so to speak.

The other part of [I]NFB[/I] is the visual novel, depicting your family life in between prominent shifts at the television station. It is in this section that you see how your relationships with various family members, as well as with your boss, are affected by the change in government, government policies, the decisions that you’ve made at work.

The visual novel is not bad, just not as dynamic, interesting and funny as the vision mixing portion. This shift in tone may be intentional, reminding players that while this game is a satire, the actions of government and media do have an impact on people’s lives in the “real” world. Yet, I found this reminder was more poignantly conveyed in one of the later chapters in the vision mixing portion. Besides, I never found myself caring about my in-game family or boss enough to worry about what they think.

[H2]The Acting: [/H2]
UK gamers and/or those who are familiar with UK television may recognize a few faces among the cast. I was at first a bit skeptical about Paul Baverstock’s casting as a news anchor, but he immediately won me over as the disenchanted, surly Jeremy Donaldson after just one scene. Andrea Vall was charismatic as the ambitious Megan Wolfe; Roger Alborough was natural as the foul-mouthed Peter Clement; and Claire Rackyleft was brilliant as the smarmy Julia Salisbury. Yet, it was George Vere who chewed the scenery as the self-important, cowardly Patrick Bannon, as well as the similarly vain Graham Bannon. I found his performance to be fitting in the game’s mockery of inept journalism.

[H2]Final Thoughts: [/H2]
The hybrid of vision mixing gameplay and FMV presentation makes [I]NFB[/I] a unique game in the dystopian adventure genre. Its gameplay mechanics engage players in reflection on the power of media in shaping the political narratives we hear. While it’s neither pro-left nor pro-right, it does tell a cautionary tale of political extremism. Even if you disregard the commentary, [I]NFB[/I] offers fun, challenging gameplay as well as blunt satire that make this game worth checking out.

Not For Broadcast is a great concept executed really well. It's funny, it's clever, it's stressful in the best way. I played through the whole thing on deck and it's totally doable, but definitely play it with a keyboard if you can. I'd recommend this to anyone.

It's fun at the start, but after a while I started to get bored, and it wasn't fun anymore because they added too many things, like cuddly bear monsters climbing up poles and having to zap them off, and cuddly bear monsters jumping through you window and messing with your buttons if you don't hit them away. I would recommend buying it while its on sale if your not sure you want it, or you've just watched a few YouTube videos on it and thought it looks fun.

A great concept that very quickly outstays it's welcome. I really enjoyed the first 20 mins, half an hour. It's a unique concept.

However, the concept quickly gets old, after that it's like watching a college high school doing skits. Fine. Nothing terrible. But unless your their mum or a friend come along to support, it's half a chore to sit through.

That is exacerbated by the fact it's a skill challenge game that relies on you to sit through the same extended dialogue and clips multiple times, especially if you want to get achievements, challenges or the different endings. A skit that probably stood up to a first watch, becomes absolutely painful when you're listening to it for the third, fifth, 10th time, trying to get through various sections or combos.

Great cast and acting, and the actual video mixing is a blast. Too bad it’s all wrapped around a smug centrist take where you’re the idiot (the actual player not your cleaner turned broadcast controller character) for believing anything.  I can’t stress that enough, the story is a both-sides satire so desperate to look clever that it gaslights you as the game bends over backwards to make you feel like an idiot no matter what you do.

Outside of the story, BTW this is a story heavy game, the actual gameplay drowns you in so much busywork that you miss the dialogue, then you’re forced to re-watch 10 minutes of clips you mostly already saw or heard in a different menu. (While there is a fast-forward option, they pitch the audio so you can barely understand it unless you play it at 1x speed, and there are usually multiple different clips going at the same time. So, goody, time to pad out that playtime unless you’re okay with just not actually understanding the game.) Between the broadcasts there’s this really terrible “life-sim” that only reason to exist is to just make your life worse and punishing you for not following a steam guide and is just a slog to go through. Honestly, it’s so cheap looking compared to the rest of the game that it feels slapped together at the last minute with no budget, and it shouldn’t have been in the game; there could’ve been other ways to show the effects without bringing the game to a screeching halt.

I can’t imagine trying to do multiple playthroughs as playing it once is already miserable sans a few moments when you do nothing and can enjoy some banter. The acting and such as I mentioned is amazing so really just watch the broadcast clips on YouTube and enjoy yourself.

I was inspired to play this after watching Jacksepticeye play the first couple of levels. It was both hilarious and intriguing, and I really loved the gameplay. I would restart chapters over and over just to get perfect scores. Honestly, I can't really think of any negatives. It's very unique and interesting.

Worth playing for sure, but the really weird politics only felt weirder this time around. I think it would have been better and more effective if it wasn't trying to be so quirky the whole time. There are really genuine moments of pathos that are undercut by constant jokes. Plus, (despite the game clearly disliking both parties it presents) the things it decides to present as evil for Advance are... strange. Like maybe I'm just too woke but are we really still making a big deal about tax cuts for 1%ers. It really wants to portray both sides as well meaning when... I would argue frankly neither side is irl! I think a choice between truly bad and truly bad (perhaps both dressed as being nice) would have been more effective compared to the choice we get between misguided utopianism and weirdly anarchic conservatism. Would love to see a more serious version of this but also that version wouldn't have Patrick Bannon 2 which is one of my all time favorite bits in anything ever.

This game is an underrated gem! Without spoiling too much, it's a perfect blend of political dystopia and dark comedy that deserves far more attention than it has! There are many moments in this game of "Uh oh- That might be MY fault-"

Just play it, genuinely it's worth every cent.

I remember buying this a game a long time ago. It was very comical. For some odd reason steam reset my hours played on this game pretty sure i had close to over 100+ but anyways I enjoy this game very much and would recommend it to anyone who likes a challenge that makes them use their quick wits and brain to get a task done. As of right now I'm focusing on completing every single achievement in the game and I'm well on my way to getting that done for this game. This game is really fun, especially if you love puzzle/time management games with multiple things happening at once.  Soothes my ADHD brain.

This is just a brilliant game from start to finish to the point that it's unprecedented in its genre and approach. What stands out about it is the sheer creativity that harmonizes a direct and brutal dark humor (no doubt that it will be created by the British) with a keen satire to the point of perfection.

The amount of thought process, great writing, superb acting, awesome scores and tedious editing to make it work is mind boggling. Even though the game gives the player a kind of 80s-set environment vibe, what it aims to carry its focal point in terms of ridiculing meshed with full-fledged critique still resembles how pitiful media has turned into at this age. It is so that, I've seen parts where the creators' intention being the whole idea should be seen as absurd and scoffed at actually happened right before my eyes over the past few years. 

There are minor issues like the imprecise ideology of Advance that felt to me slided over hastily a bit, or improvement of a more sound grading system of your editing, or even making a better guidelines about it would be better in general, however, none of those issues take away the games brilliancy, per se.

Overall, I have enjoyed every part of it and would definitely want to experience it more (I'll definitely try different scenarios later). The bastardization of news, inseperability of the medium and the politics, huge reduction in quality in the music, theatre, show and journalism business (essentially anything that TV can offer) could not have been explained and mocked better with a plain awareness in a game. 

10/10

Conceptually interesting with incredible actor performances, the game is let down massively by mediocre game design and political commentary that edges into insulting. Your ability to make influencing decisions is restricted to discrete moments during a broadcast (play an opposition tape or don't, censor anti-government commentary or don't) or in strange interstitials between broadcasts that take place at home, akin to a visual novel. It is impossible for your broadcasts to be involved in any amount of subtle agenda setting, as it would be in the real world, because you are constantly assessed by the game as to whether or not your choices of shot are sufficiently audience retaining. For example, broadcasting a topless woman protesting next to the authoritarian Prime Minister will have no effect on political outcomes because the game determines those shots to be the "Not For Broadcast" (it says as much in the game over screen) and your game will simply end if you attempt to show them. You are penalized if you linger on a shot for too long, even if any other shot that the game wants you to broadcast would be inappropriate or inconsistent with the overarching themes of the story: the built-in assessor overrides any plot nuance that could be expressed through more intelligent game design decisions. Given this, the agenda setting potential of mainstream media is barely able to be explored. Instead, you are mostly just tasked with keeping the game's rudimentary audience meter in the green as a couple of annoying minigames fight for your attention from time-to-time. It is shame that a concept with such potential was executed so poorly. That said, the actor performances were outstanding and were, by far, the most impressive part of the game.

One of my favorites games ever!! The story is really silly and funny at the beginning, but it starts to feel more serious as you go forward and make decisions. The actors are amazing and I enjoy so much playing it every time!! Highly recommend it <3

Fantastic, maybe 3-4 hours of game play here (2 plays with the current content) as of 2/6/2020 but I am looking forward to experiencing the full game - more than once!

Ready for more!

I really enjoy this game's mechanics and pace. However there are some issues with the content that make playing it kind of a bummer.

The narrative's reliance on hacky, sometimes offensive comedy tropes weakens what could be a really groundbreaking experience. I think these tropes also hinder the game's message, so far as one can be discerned (as the game tends toward ridiculing whoever it can). In the first three game segments, we have:

	1. A group of stereotypical theater kids. Included are a preening, flamboyant young man, a vapid, self-obsessed blonde, an over-eager social justice warrior type, and an intellectually disabled young man whose inability to navigate a sleeve is played for cheap laughs. 

	2. A black man, recently released from prison, offering systemic critiques of the justice system while partying with strippers and a mariachi band. 

	3. Government programs funding the arts and infrastructure are depicted as stupid or vaguely sinister boondoggles. 

I just think in 2020 this sort of writing is lazier than it needs to be. It's especially glaring in light of the narrative's strengths. The game, through its mechanics and narrative, reveals that those who work in media often have a financial incentive to portray individuals and organizations in a positive or negative light. The game's politics are often cute enough to carry the weaker segments; the recently dispossessed rich are played up as spoiled toffs with stupid accents, government critics are depicted as philanderers and police advocates hypocrites, celebrity politicians are liars and drunks. The news anchors are satisfyingly snide and self-absorbed. This is a real highlight of the experience for me. 

I genuinely like parts of this game so much, it's a real pain in my ass to sit through jokes that would've been stale in the 90s. ("Math's really important!" "Okay [intellectually disabled young man]. " "Math's really important!" "Yeah okay [intellectually disabled young man].") I also feel like, if I were disabled, or a person of color, I'd probably be doing more than wincing through these segments.

At the end of the released Early Access segments, the devs say they read these reviews, that they read everything. To be clear, the game does have some aspects I think are thoughtful. These include gender neutral names for the protagonist and their partner, a consistently scathing take on capitalist consumerism, captains of industry (Sophia Remmington is a great Elon Musk stand-in), and sports culture, and some laugh out loud funny bits of banter among the news crew. The game also manages to spoof the stupid way the media portrays scientific endeavors. My intent isn't to cancel this game, whatever that would mean. I do think, though, the devs maybe haven't considered these angles, or if they have, dismissed them too quickly. 

Maybe it's too late to influence the writing- some segments clearly have already been filmed and I am excited to watch those, to be honest- but after playing through the game so far several times, I came away feeling a little icky, and I felt like I had to express why. Hopefully the devs can dig that. I am looking forward to where this is going.

There are two reasons I don't recommend Not For Broadcast - technical issues, and tonal inconsistencies that ruin the experience. 

It will start off seeming like a better made, more in depth, live action answer to something like [i]Papers Please[/i] and you'll be quite excited to see how things go, but unfortunately the answer is nowhere good.

[i]Not For Broadcast[/i] can't seem to decide if it wants to be a cutting-room simulator where your technical skill as a live editor of a political TV show is the deciding factor, a CYOA political drama where your social and political point of view makes the difference, or a silly game about gremlins and poop jokes and hitting stuffy British TV presenters with metaphorical pies. But not only does it want to be all three it tries very hard to be all three, so hard that it ends up nowhere near any one point of the triangle but nowhere near a happy medium either. You're left with a feeling that too many people were pulling this too many directions and the end result is something that was just sort of narratively ripped to pieces in the process. 

The technical issues greatly compound this, as a game that hard crashes but reloads a few minutes back is one thing, but a game like this that hard crashes after you've just gone through a half hour of editing a scene is soul-crushing. A sane person probably would have quit after the second time it happened, but I pushed through to the end. Don't repeat my mistake here. I deleted it from steam after finally finishing. 

There was some definite talent that went into making this, so the fact that it didn't come together in the end is a shame, but I don't recommend it any price.

I really wanted to like this game. I really did. The idea of sitting in a broadcast booth, shaping the narrative that determines the outcome of perception is such a great mechanic for storytelling. But sadly the story itself is so fascicle it borders on insulting. What tries to be a commentary on the a dystopian future vis a vis 1984, ends up being a ham-fisted Alex Jones-esque fever dream of "Woke politics run amok". 

Your choices are to side with the bumbling but somehow simultaneously sinister antagonist political party, or to side with the wealthy autocratic protagonist society defrocked of their money and power. Both options are however portrayed as the "fallacy" of equality, the "oppression" of the wealthy, and the "indulgence" of the liberal arts. 

But these all pale in comparison to the cardinal sin of gaming: It's just not a "fun" game. There's a few laughs here and there, but it's just too busy focusing on the dangers of collective bargaining (political action, teamwork, compromise) to be enjoyable. The overall feel of the game is one very long sermon on the Calvinist ideal that the wealthy deserve their place, the marginalized and downtrodden deserve their place, and any attempt to change that will result in apocalypse and misery for all.

Whatever one's political sentiments may be, this game certainly doesn't do justice to well representing them or the effect media has on influencing them. Instead it offers a paranoid, demeaning attempt at delivering a poorly contrived "message" of individualistic supremacy for it's story, mediocre game play mechanics, annoying and unrelated mini-game gimmicks, and an overall boring experience at best, and downright insulting experience at worst.

Awesome awesome game, loved it so much. When writing this I have 41 hours, have completed the main story 4 times, and played all the DLC's. This game is not for everyone, I definitely think its a niche game and I certainly think it can fall under the title of interactive movie, but not in a bad way by any means. 

First thing I would say if you buy this game: PLAY IT ON STORY MODE! Try the other difficulties at some point just to see the mechanics and those parts of the game, but for me personally, things like interference, overheating, and the other things that pop up, I just found them annoying and distracting from an otherwise awesome story being played by real actors who clearly care about and had so much fun with what the character they were playing. A friend once described it as "Adult Swim energy" while watching me play and I thought it fit very well.

The game goes on sale for $6 for the main story, and $10 for all the DLC included. The main story alone is a great time, and if you do like the main story, all the DLC is fun, especially The Timeloop. I was pleasantly surprised how much we got in The Timeloop and all the wacky stuff we got to see. Even the DLC's have multiple endings you can get.

My biggest points would be: I do think its a niche game, not for everyone, but if you think it looks cool give it a shot. I had a ton of fun and laughed so much. And PLAY THE GAME ON STORY MODE! Pay attention to the characters, get immersed in their stories and in the world. I enjoyed the game much more when I did just watch as a movie rather than dealing with all the side mechanics. For $10 for all the DLC, you should have a great time.

The difficulty can be a little challenging but, over all best game I have have played in 2020, and I am sure after early access and once episode two is out it will be even better! So get it now while it's in early access and support this amazing game in its development!

This is such a fascinating game. I'm not usually someone who cares about getting multiple endings, this is the first time I've wanted to get as many as possible. What an interesting--and ultimately somewhat frustrating--game. Not for Broadcast is an innovative take on the FMV and propaganda sim genres, putting you in charge of a broadcast room on the eve of political upheaval. It's at times quite clever, and often funny, and even more often absolutely strange in a delightful way. But it ultimately fails as a satire, I think, because the politics are utterly incoherent. It's unclear who its targets are and any possible attempts at having something meaningful to say are undercut by presenting a set of actors who are uniformly unsympathetic. Every idea is treated as ridiculous and worthy of ridicule -- and hey, maybe that's fair to some extent -- but the satire lacks teeth because it doesn't feel grounded in anything real. I can attempt to read it as a right-libertarian takedown of leftist politics, but it doesn't really even work as that. Or maybe it's meant to "make fun of everyone," I don't know. But it doesn't really work in that mode, either.

All that said, I really enjoyed playing the game. The mechanics are unique, sort of a mix of rhythm game and stress nightmare (in the best way), and the game is legitimately well-acted and, at points, really, really funny in its absurdity. I was consistently impressed by how good the actors were and how real the performances felt, even as the satirical bits felt unmoored. It's fun to run the vision mixer and twiddle knobs and censor swears and all of that, and it's clear that each play through can be pretty unique.

That leads to my last criticism, however, which is that with four different paths, each with 3-4 different endings, you end up with fourteen possible endings. And that's just too many. I just can't imagine wanting to play the game that many times to get to check out all the various epilogues. And believe me, I am curious about them! But, as fun as the game is, after finishing I'm not particularly excited to play it all over again. And again. And again. And again. And again. And so on ...

In all, a really cool concept that's well executed on most levels somewhat hampered by incoherent political storytelling.

It's a good game and does a good job of showing how the news can sway the public to believe one narrative over another. Can't wait for the next season to get finished so I can watch a fictional world collapse alongside our own! 
The only think I don't like is that I know it will end
8/10

Amazing game, probably one of the most engaging & fun games I've ever played. The broadcasting mechanics might be a bit tedious at times but its all worth it to see the story unfold. The fact that the base game has so many different branching paths and endings adds a great deal of replayability but not being able to skip certain already played segments hinders it. I have a love for unique games and this hit all the right notes.

If you like the charm of old FMV games, absurdist humour and games with political commentary, I recommend playing Not for Broadcast. There's hours of recorded content, it's genuinely impressive how much is packed into this game for its price, and the actors' performances are great!

I will say, if you're expecting super insightful political commentary (at least from a left-wing perspective anyway) this game doesn't really have that. The focus is more on the effects of propoganda and how the media shapes the masses, rather than delving into any one political faction, and tends to favour centrism as the best outcome. This isn't a dealbreaker or anything, I did find their approach to politics something different compared to what you might see in the real world, which made it more interesting in my opinion. 

Really it's just a fun game. I recommend playing it several times, trying different outcomes, seeing all the endings. Play the DLCs too! It's just a great time all around.

This could be a great game, but sometimes failing broadcasts for silly reasons, and having to replay a 10 minute segment, is too much. Checkpoints should be much more frequent to avoid having to replay entire chapters for something silly. Some of the mechanics just seem to be a waste of effort. Would prefer to just watch a playthrough on YouTube.
